statement: Let $F$ be a [number field](c:number-field). Every [irreducible representation](c:irreducible-representation) of the [adelic group](c:adelic-group) $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{A}_F)$ occurs at most once in the space $L^2_{\mathrm{cusp}}$ of square-integrable cusp forms on $\mathrm{GL}_n(F)\backslash \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{A}_F)$.

hypotheses.text: $F$ is a [number field](c:number-field) with adele ring $\mathbb{A}_F$, and $n \ge 1$.

The space is $L^2_{\mathrm{cusp}}$, the closed subspace of [cusp forms](c:cusp-form) in $L^2(\mathrm{GL}_n(F)\backslash \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{A}_F))$, and $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{A}_F)$ acts by right translation.
The representation $\pi$ is an [irreducible representation](c:irreducible-representation) that occurs in $L^2_{\mathrm{cusp}}$ as a closed invariant subspace.

conclusion: Two closed invariant subspaces of $L^2_{\mathrm{cusp}}$ that are both isomorphic to $\pi$ are equal, so the multiplicity of $\pi$ is $0$ or $1$ and each cuspidal [automorphic representation](c:automorphic-representation) sits in $L^2_{\mathrm{cusp}}$ in one way.

proofs.name: Whittaker models (Shalika)
proofs.slogan: A cusp form is determined by its Whittaker function, and Whittaker functionals on an irreducible representation are unique up to a scalar.
proofs.scope: All $n \ge 1$ and the whole cuspidal spectrum; the family also holds strong multiplicity one, which this outline does not cover. The steps outline the cited paper.

roles.why: The field fixes the adele ring and the unipotent subgroups of the Fourier expansion.
Cuspidality removes the degenerate Fourier terms, so a cusp form equals its Whittaker series.
Irreducibility makes $\pi$ a restricted tensor product, so local uniqueness gives global uniqueness.

steps.slogan: Expand each cusp form in its Whittaker-Fourier series.
steps.detail: For a cusp form $\varphi$ and a fixed nondegenerate character $\psi$, the Fourier expansion along the unipotent radical (Piatetski-Shapiro, Shalika) gives $\varphi(g)=\sum_{\gamma \in N_{n-1}(F)\backslash \mathrm{GL}_{n-1}(F)} W_\varphi(\mathrm{diag}(\gamma,1)g)$. Cuspidality removes all other terms. Here $W_\varphi$ is the [Whittaker function](c:whittaker-function) of $\varphi$.

steps.slogan: Show that a cusp form with zero Whittaker function is zero.
steps.detail: If $W_\varphi=0$, the expansion gives $\varphi=0$. So $\varphi \mapsto W_\varphi$ is injective on $L^2_{\mathrm{cusp}}$, and it commutes with right translation.

steps.slogan: Turn the Whittaker coefficient into a Whittaker functional on $\pi$.
steps.detail: On a copy $V$ of $\pi$ in $L^2_{\mathrm{cusp}}$, the map $\Lambda(\varphi)=W_\varphi(1)$ is a $(N(\mathbb{A}_F),\psi)$-equivariant functional, nonzero by injectivity, and $W_\varphi(g)=\Lambda(\pi(g)\varphi)$. The representation $\pi$ is a restricted tensor product $\otimes'_v \pi_v$ of local representations.

steps.slogan: Quote uniqueness of local Whittaker functionals at every place.
steps.detail: At each place $v$ the space of $(N(F_v),\psi_v)$-Whittaker functionals on $\pi_v$ has dimension at most one (Gelfand-Kazhdan, Shalika). So global Whittaker functionals on $\pi$ form a space of dimension at most one.

steps.slogan: Compare two copies of $\pi$ through their Whittaker functionals.
steps.detail: Let $T\colon V_1 \to V_2$ be an isomorphism of two copies. Uniqueness gives $\Lambda_2\circ T=c\Lambda_1$ with $c \ne 0$, hence $W_{T\varphi}=cW_\varphi$ for all $\varphi$. Injectivity gives $T\varphi=c\varphi$, so $V_2=V_1$.

concepts.c:number-field: The field fixes the adele ring and the unipotent groups of the expansion.
concepts.c:irreducible-representation: Irreducibility makes $\pi$ a restricted tensor product with unique local models.
concepts.c:adelic-group: The adelic group acts on cusp forms and is a restricted product of local groups.
concepts.c:automorphic-representation: Cuspidal automorphic representations are the irreducible pieces whose multiplicity the theorem counts.
concepts.c:cusp-form: Cuspidality removes degenerate Fourier terms, so the Whittaker coefficient determines the form.
concepts.c:whittaker-function: The Whittaker function of a cusp form determines the form.

source.ref: J. A. Shalika, The multiplicity one theorem for GL_n, Annals of Mathematics (2) 100 (1974), 171-193
source.note: Shalika proves local uniqueness of Whittaker models and that cusp forms are determined by their Whittaker functions; the outline follows his argument.

statement: Let $\Psi(t)=\sum \Psi_n t^n$ have $\Psi_n>0$ with $\Psi_{n+1}/\Psi_n$ decreasing to $0$, and let $f(z)=\sum f_n z^n$ be a [power series](c:power-series). The infimum $\tau$ of all $B$ with $|f(z)|\le A\,\Psi(B|z|)$ for some $A$ equals $\limsup |f_n/\Psi_n|^{1/n}$. For $\Psi=e^t$ this is [exponential type](c:function-of-exponential-type).

hypotheses.text: The coefficients satisfy $\Psi_n>0$, and the ratios $\Psi_{n+1}/\Psi_n$ decrease to $0$ (for $e^t$ they are $1/(n+1)$).
$f(z)=\sum_{n\ge 0} f_n z^n$ is a [power series](c:power-series) with complex coefficients.

conclusion: The type $\tau$ equals $L=\limsup |f_n/\Psi_n|^{1/n}$, so the generalized [Borel transform](c:borel-transform) $\sum f_n/(\Psi_n w^{n+1})$ converges for $|w|>\tau$ and diverges for $|w|<\tau$.

proofs.name: Cauchy estimates
proofs.slogan: A coefficient bound gives the growth bound termwise, and a Cauchy estimate at a well-chosen radius gives the coefficient bound back.
proofs.scope: The comparison functions with decreasing ratios; the case $\Psi=e^t$, $\Psi_n=1/n!$ is the classical exponential type. If $L=\infty$, no bound of the form $A\Psi(B|z|)$ exists and $\tau=\infty$.

roles.why: Decreasing ratios let the sum at the chosen radius be compared with its largest term.
The coefficients are the data of both inequalities and give the Borel series.

steps.slogan: Bound $f$ by $\Psi$ when the upper limit $L$ is finite.
steps.detail: For every $B>L$ there is $C$ with $|f_n|\le C B^n\Psi_n$ for all $n$. Summing gives $|f(z)|\le C\,\Psi(B|z|)$ for all $z$, so $\tau\le L$.

steps.slogan: Apply the Cauchy estimate to a given growth bound.
steps.detail: Assume $|f(z)|\le A\,\Psi(B|z|)$ for all $z$. Then $f$ is [entire](c:entire-function), and the Cauchy estimate on $|z|=r$ gives $|f_n|\le A\,\Psi(Br)/r^n$ for every $r>0$.

steps.slogan: Estimate the terms of $\Psi(Br)/r^n$ at the radius $Br=1/((1+\epsilon)\rho_n)$.
steps.detail: Put $\rho_k=\Psi_{k+1}/\Psi_k$. Decreasing ratios give $\Psi_k\le\Psi_n\rho_n^{k-n}$ for $k\ge n$ and $\Psi_k\le\Psi_n\rho_n^{-(n-k)}$ for $k<n$. The terms with $k\ge n$ sum to at most $\Psi_n(1+\epsilon)/\epsilon$ times $B^n$, and the $n$ other terms are at most $(1+\epsilon)^n\Psi_n B^n$ each.

steps.slogan: Take $n$-th roots and let $\epsilon$ tend to zero.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give $|f_n|\le A B^n\Psi_n\,(n(1+\epsilon)^n+(1+\epsilon)/\epsilon)$. So $L\le B(1+\epsilon)$ for all $\epsilon>0$, hence $L\le B$ for every admissible $B$. Thus $L\le\tau$, and with step 1, $\tau=L$.

steps.slogan: Read the convergence of the Borel transform from Cauchy-Hadamard.
steps.detail: In $u=1/w$ the [Borel transform](c:borel-transform) is the power series $\sum (f_n/\Psi_n)u^{n+1}$ with [radius of convergence](c:radius-of-convergence) $1/L$. So it converges for $|w|>L=\tau$ and diverges for $|w|<\tau$.

concepts.c:power-series: The proof compares the coefficients $f_n$ with the coefficients $\Psi_n$.
concepts.c:function-of-exponential-type: The case $\Psi=e^t$ is the classical exponential type.
concepts.c:entire-function: A growth bound for all $z$ makes $f$ entire, so Cauchy estimates apply.
concepts.c:borel-transform: Its convergence domain is what the type $\tau$ determines.
concepts.c:radius-of-convergence: Cauchy-Hadamard turns the limit superior into the convergence radius.

source.note: Direct Cauchy and Cauchy-Hadamard argument for comparison functions with decreasing coefficient ratios; for $\Psi=e^t$ it is the classical statement on exponential type.

statement: Every [Stein manifold](c:stein-manifold) of dimension $n$ admits an injective proper [holomorphic immersion](c:holomorphic-immersion) into $\mathbb{C}^{2n+1}$, that is, a closed holomorphic embedding.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a [Stein manifold](c:stein-manifold) of complex dimension $n$.

conclusion: There is a holomorphic map $F\colon X\to\mathbb{C}^{2n+1}$ that is injective, a [proper map](c:proper-map), and an immersion at every point.

proofs.name: Embedding and projection
proofs.slogan: Embed the Stein manifold properly in some $\mathbb{C}^N$, then project down one dimension at a time while keeping injectivity, immersion and properness.
proofs.scope: Every $n \ge 1$; the outline names the ingredients of the cited work, which also treats Stein spaces with singularities.

roles.why: Holomorphic convexity gives an exhaustion, and Cartan's theorems give many global functions.

steps.slogan: Exhaust the manifold by holomorphically convex compact sets.
steps.detail: A [Stein manifold](c:stein-manifold) is holomorphically convex, so it has compact sets $K_j$ with $K_j\subset\mathrm{int}K_{j+1}$ whose union is $X$ and which are convex with respect to the algebra of global holomorphic functions. Holomorphic functions near $K_j$ are approximated by global ones.

steps.slogan: Build a proper injective immersion into some $\mathbb{C}^N$.
steps.detail: Cartan's Theorems A and B give global holomorphic functions that separate points and tangent vectors on each $K_j$. Adding functions that grow along the exhaustion yields a holomorphic map $X\to\mathbb{C}^N$ that is injective, proper and an [immersion](c:holomorphic-immersion), for $N$ large.

steps.slogan: Show that a generic linear projection keeps injectivity and immersion.
steps.detail: The secant directions $[F(x)-F(y)]$ and tangent directions form images of manifolds of complex dimension at most $2n$ in $\mathbb{P}^{N-1}$. If $N-1>2n$, Sard's theorem gives a direction outside them, so the projection to $\mathbb{C}^{N-1}$ is still an injective immersion.

steps.slogan: Perturb the map so that the projection stays proper.
steps.detail: A projection can lose properness. The cited work corrects this by Runge-type approximation along the exhaustion: it adds small holomorphic terms on each $K_j$ so that the projected map still tends to infinity at the ends of $X$.

steps.slogan: Repeat the projection until the target is $\mathbb{C}^{2n+1}$.
steps.detail: Each round lowers $N$ by one while $N-1>2n$, that is while $N\ge 2n+2$. The last round ends at $N-1=2n+1$ and gives the injective proper immersion into $\mathbb{C}^{2n+1}$.

concepts.c:stein-manifold: Holomorphic convexity of the manifold supplies the exhaustion and the global functions.
concepts.c:holomorphic-immersion: Immersion at every point is preserved by generic projections.
concepts.c:proper-map: Properness makes the image closed and the map an embedding.

source.ref: R. Narasimhan, Imbedding of holomorphically complete complex spaces, American Journal of Mathematics 82 (1960), 917-934
source.note: Narasimhan proves the injective proper immersion into C^{2n+1} for Stein manifolds; the embedding is also credited to Remmert and Bishop.

statement: In a [tangential quadrilateral](c:tangential-quadrilateral) $ABCD$ that is not a rhombus, the center $I$ of the [incircle](c:incircle) lies on the Newton line, the line through the [midpoints](c:midpoint) $M$ of $AC$ and $N$ of $BD$.

hypotheses.text: $ABCD$ is a convex [tangential quadrilateral](c:tangential-quadrilateral): its four sides touch a circle with center $I$ and radius $r$.
$ABCD$ is not a rhombus.

conclusion: The midpoints satisfy $M\ne N$, and the points $I$, $M$, $N$ are collinear.

proofs.name: Signed area function
proofs.slogan: The signed-area difference $f$ is an affine function that vanishes at $I$, $M$ and $N$, so $I$ lies on the line $MN$.
proofs.scope: Convex tangential quadrilaterals. The case $M=N$ is exactly the rhombus, where the Newton line is undefined.

roles.why: Equal tangent lengths give Pitot's equation, and the radius $r$ gives the areas of the four triangles at $I$.
It excludes a parallelogram, so $f$ is not constant and $M\ne N$.

steps.slogan: Equate the sums of opposite sides.
steps.detail: The two tangent segments from each vertex have equal length, so $AB+CD=BC+DA$.

steps.slogan: Show that $I$ has equal sums of opposite triangle areas.
steps.detail: Each triangle $IAB$, $IBC$, $ICD$, $IDA$ has height $r$ over its side, so $[IAB]+[ICD]=\tfrac12 r(AB+CD)=\tfrac12 r(BC+DA)=[IBC]+[IDA]$. With signed [areas](c:area) for the order $A,B,C,D$, this says $f(I)=0$ for $f(P)=[PAB]+[PCD]-[PBC]-[PDA]$.

steps.slogan: Show that $f$ is an affine function of $P$.
steps.detail: Since $[PXY]=\tfrac12(X\times Y+P\times(X-Y))$, we get $f(P)=\kappa+P\times(A-B+C-D)$ with $\kappa$ a constant. So $f$ is affine, and it is constant exactly when $A+C=B+D$, that is, when $M=N$.

steps.slogan: Check that $f$ vanishes at $M$ and at $N$.
steps.detail: For $M=(A+C)/2$ affinity gives $[MAB]=\tfrac12[CAB]$, $[MCD]=\tfrac12[ACD]$, $[MBC]=\tfrac12[ABC]$ and $[MDA]=\tfrac12[CDA]$. Cyclic order gives $[CAB]=[ABC]$ and $[CDA]=[ACD]$, so $f(M)=0$. The same computation gives $f(N)=0$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $I$ lies on the zero line of $f$, which is the line $MN$.
steps.detail: If $M=N$, the diagonals bisect each other, so $ABCD$ is a [parallelogram](c:parallelogram) and Pitot's equation gives $AB=BC$: a rhombus. So $M\ne N$, $f$ is a nonconstant affine function, and its zero set is a line through $M$, $N$ and $I$.

concepts.c:tangential-quadrilateral: Equal tangent lengths give Pitot's equation and the incenter.
concepts.c:incircle: Its radius gives the areas of the four triangles at $I$.
concepts.c:midpoint: The diagonal midpoints $M$ and $N$ define the Newton line.
concepts.c:area: Signed areas turn the incenter condition into one affine equation.
concepts.c:parallelogram: A tangential parallelogram is a rhombus, the excluded case.

source.note: Standard proof: the locus of points with equal sums of opposite triangle areas is the Newton line; Pitot's theorem puts the incenter on it.

statement: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with [parallelograms](c:parallelogram) $CAFG$ and $CBDE$ attached outside on $CA$ and $CB$. Let $H$ be where the lines $FG$ and $DE$ meet. The parallelogram on $AB$ with other sides parallel and equal to $HC$ has [area](c:area) equal to the sum of the other two areas.

hypotheses.text: $ABC$ is a nondegenerate [triangle](c:triangle).
$CAFG$ and $CBDE$ are [parallelograms](c:parallelogram) on $CA$ and $CB$ that lie outside the triangle.
$H$ is the point where the lines $FG$ and $DE$ meet.

conclusion: The parallelogram on $AB$ with sides parallel and equal to $HC$ has area $[CAFG]+[CBDE]$.

proofs.name: Vectors and shear
proofs.slogan: Shear each outer parallelogram so that its free side becomes $\vec{CH}$, then add the two areas as one cross product.
proofs.scope: Parallelograms attached outside the triangle. For squares the theorem gives the Pythagorean theorem; the proof does not use it.

roles.why: Independent sides $a,b$ make the two outer lines meet and fix the orientation.
Outside placement fixes the signs of the two cross products.
The point $H$ gives the common vector $h$ that replaces both free sides.

steps.slogan: Place $C$ at the origin and name the side vectors.
steps.detail: Let $a=\vec{CA}$, $b=\vec{CB}$, $u=\vec{CG}$, $v=\vec{CE}$, with $a\times b>0$. The areas are $|a\times u|$ and $|b\times v|$. Outside placement means $a\times u<0$ and $b\times v>0$.

steps.slogan: Write $H$ on both outer lines.
steps.detail: The line $FG$ is $\{u+sa\}$ and the line $DE$ is $\{v+tb\}$. Since $a,b$ are independent, they meet in one point with $h=\vec{CH}=u+sa=v+tb$.

steps.slogan: Replace each free side by $h$ without changing the area.
steps.detail: We have $a\times u=a\times(h-sa)=a\times h$ and $b\times v=b\times(h-tb)=b\times h$. This is a [shear](c:shear-map): sliding a free side along its own line keeps the cross product.

steps.slogan: Add the two cross products to get the third area.
steps.detail: Since $a\times h<0<b\times h$, we get $(b-a)\times h=|b\times v|+|a\times u|$. The left side is the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\vec{AB}=b-a$ and $h=\vec{CH}$.

concepts.c:triangle: Its two sides at $C$ are independent vectors.
concepts.c:parallelogram: Each parallelogram has area equal to a cross product of two sides.
concepts.c:area: The theorem is an equation between areas.
concepts.c:shear-map: A shear keeps the area while moving the free side to $\vec{CH}$.

source.note: Direct proof with cross products: an area-preserving shear moves each free side to the vector $CH$.

statement: In a circle, let $H$ be the side of the inscribed regular [hexagon](c:hexagon) and $D$ the side of the inscribed regular decagon. Then $H^2=D(H+D)$, so $H/D=\varphi$, the [golden ratio](c:golden-ratio).

hypotheses.text: A circle of radius $R$ holds an inscribed regular [hexagon](c:hexagon) with side $H$ and an inscribed regular decagon with side $D$.

proofs.name: Isosceles triangle of the decagon
proofs.slogan: Bisect a base angle of the isosceles triangle with apex angle $36^\circ$ to get a similar triangle, and solve the proportion.
proofs.scope: The inscribed polygons share one circle. This is the golden ratio identity used in Euclid's proof of the pentagon, decagon and hexagon identity.

roles.why: The common radius $R$ equals the hexagon side and is the leg of the decagon triangle.

steps.slogan: Show that the hexagon side equals the radius.
steps.detail: Adjacent vertices $A',B'$ of the hexagon and the center $O$ give a triangle with $OA'=OB'=R$ and apex angle $60^\circ$. It is an [equilateral triangle](c:equilateral-triangle), so $H=R$.

steps.slogan: Draw the isosceles triangle of one decagon side.
steps.detail: For adjacent decagon vertices $A,B$ and the center $O$, we have $OA=OB=R$ and $\angle AOB=36^\circ$. So the base angles are $72^\circ$ and $AB=D$.

steps.slogan: Bisect the base angle at $A$ and name the new point $C$.
steps.detail: The bisector meets $OB$ at $C$. Then $\angle CAB=36^\circ$ and $\angle ACB=72^\circ$, so $AC=AB=D$. Also $\angle OAC=\angle AOC=36^\circ$, so $OC=AC=D$ and $CB=R-D$.

steps.slogan: Compare the triangles $ABC$ and $OAB$.
steps.detail: Both have angles $36^\circ,72^\circ,72^\circ$, so they are [similar triangles](c:similar-triangles). Hence $AB/OA=CB/AB$, that is, $D/R=(R-D)/D$.

steps.slogan: Solve the proportion and identify the golden ratio.
steps.detail: We get $D^2=R(R-D)$, so $R^2=D(R+D)$, and with $H=R$ this is $H^2=D(H+D)$. Then $x=H/D$ solves $x^2=x+1$, and its positive root is the [golden ratio](c:golden-ratio) $(1+\sqrt5)/2$.

concepts.c:hexagon: The hexagon side equals the radius, which fixes the scale.
concepts.c:equilateral-triangle: The central triangle of a hexagon side is equilateral.
concepts.c:similar-triangles: Similarity of the two $36$-$72$-$72$ triangles gives the proportion.

source.note: Angle chase after Euclid, Elements XIII.9 (the golden triangle).

statement: Let $ABC$ be an [equilateral triangle](c:equilateral-triangle) and $P$ a point of its plane. Then $PA\le PB+PC$, $PB\le PC+PA$ and $PC\le PA+PB$, so the distances $PA,PB,PC$ are the sides of a possibly degenerate triangle.

hypotheses.text: $ABC$ is an [equilateral triangle](c:equilateral-triangle).
$P$ is any point in the plane of $ABC$.

conclusion: Each of $PA$, $PB$, $PC$ is at most the sum of the other two.

proofs.name: Rotation by 60 degrees
proofs.slogan: Rotate $P$ by $60^\circ$ about $B$ so that the three distances become the sides of a triangle $APP'$.
proofs.scope: The three inequalities for every $P$. If $P$ is on the circumcircle the triangle is degenerate, and if $P=B$ then $P'=P$.

roles.why: Equal sides and $60^\circ$ angles make the rotation about $B$ carry $C$ to $A$.
The point $P$ has an image $P'$ whose distances to $A$, $P$ and $B$ are the three lengths.

steps.slogan: Rotate the plane about $B$ so that $C$ goes to $A$.
steps.detail: Since $BC=BA$ and $\angle CBA=60^\circ$, a [rotation](c:rotation) $\rho$ by $60^\circ$ about $B$ has $\rho(C)=A$. Put $P'=\rho(P)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the triangle $BPP'$ is equilateral.
steps.detail: We have $BP'=BP$ and $\angle PBP'=60^\circ$, so $PP'=PB$. If $P=B$ then $P'=P$ and $PP'=0=PB$.

steps.slogan: Transfer the length $PC$ to the segment $AP'$.
steps.detail: A rotation keeps distances, so $AP'=\rho(C)\rho(P)$ has length $CP$. Hence the third side of the triangle $APP'$ has length $PC$.

steps.slogan: Apply the triangle inequality to the points $A$, $P$, $P'$.
steps.detail: The points $A,P,P'$ have mutual distances $AP$, $PP'=PB$ and $P'A=PC$. The three triangle inequalities for them are the three claimed inequalities.

concepts.c:equilateral-triangle: Equal sides and $60^\circ$ angles make the rotation carry $C$ to $A$.
concepts.c:rotation: A rotation keeps distances and builds the triangle $APP'$.

proofs.name: Ptolemy's inequality
proofs.slogan: Ptolemy's inequality for the four points $A,B,C,P$ gives each inequality after division by the common side length.
proofs.scope: All $P$ in the plane. By the equality case of Ptolemy's theorem, the triangle is degenerate exactly when $P$ lies on the circumcircle.

roles.why: Equal side lengths let the common factor $s$ cancel from Ptolemy's inequality.
The point $P$ is the fourth point in the identity of differences.

steps.slogan: Write the identity of three products of differences.
steps.detail: For complex numbers $a,b,c,p$, expansion of the three products shows $(p-a)(b-c)+(p-b)(c-a)+(p-c)(a-b)=0$. Each term cancels against another term.

steps.slogan: Take absolute values to get Ptolemy's inequality.
steps.detail: The triangle inequality for complex numbers gives $|p-a||b-c|\le|p-b||c-a|+|p-c||a-b|$, which is Ptolemy's inequality for the four points.

steps.slogan: Divide by the common side length $s$ and permute the vertices.
steps.detail: In the [equilateral triangle](c:equilateral-triangle) $|b-c|=|c-a|=|a-b|=s>0$, so $PA\le PB+PC$. The same argument with the vertices permuted gives the other two inequalities.

concepts.c:equilateral-triangle: Its three equal sides let the common factor cancel.

source.note: Ptolemy's inequality from the complex identity of three products of differences.

statement: Let $M$ be a [closed manifold](c:closed-manifold) of dimension $n\ge1$ and $f\colon M\to\mathbb{R}$ a smooth [Morse function](c:morse-function) with exactly two [critical points](c:critical-point). Then $M$ is homeomorphic to the [sphere](c:sphere) $S^n$.

hypotheses.text: $M$ is a [closed manifold](c:closed-manifold): a compact smooth manifold of dimension $n\ge1$ without boundary.
$f$ is a smooth [Morse function](c:morse-function): all its critical points are nondegenerate.
$f$ has exactly two [critical points](c:critical-point).

proofs.name: Two disks glued
proofs.slogan: The two critical points are the minimum and the maximum, so $M$ is two closed balls joined by a product region, hence two balls glued along their boundary.
proofs.scope: All $n\ge1$; for $n=0$ the two critical points are the two points of $S^0$. The homeomorphism need not be a diffeomorphism.

roles.why: Compactness gives the extreme points, and properness of $f$ gives the product region.
Nondegenerate extrema have normal forms $a+|x|^2$ and $b-|y|^2$.
With only two critical points, the extrema are the critical points and the middle region has none.

steps.slogan: Identify the two critical points as the minimum and the maximum.
steps.detail: As $M$ is compact, $f$ has a minimum at some $p$ and a maximum at some $q$, and both are critical. If $p=q$, then $f$ is constant and all points are critical, which is false. So $a=f(p)<b=f(q)$, and no other point is critical.

steps.slogan: Straighten $f$ near $p$ and $q$ with the Morse lemma.
steps.detail: A [nondegenerate critical point](c:nondegenerate-critical-point) that is a minimum has index $0$, and a maximum has index $n$. The Morse lemma gives charts with $f=a+|x|^2$ near $p$ and $f=b-|y|^2$ near $q$.

steps.slogan: Cut out two closed balls around $p$ and $q$.
steps.detail: Only $p$ has $f=a$, since another such point would be a second critical point. By compactness $f^{-1}[a,a+\epsilon]$ lies in the chart for small $\epsilon$, so it is a closed ball $D_p$. In the same way $f^{-1}[b-\epsilon,b]$ is a closed ball $D_q$.

steps.slogan: Show that the region between the balls is a product $S^{n-1}\times[0,1]$ and glue.
steps.detail: On $W=f^{-1}[a+\epsilon,b-\epsilon]$ there is no critical point, so $f$ is a proper submersion onto an interval. The gradient flow, or Ehresmann's theorem, gives a [diffeomorphism](c:diffeomorph) $W\cong\partial D_p\times[0,1]$. So $M$ is $D_p$ and $D_q$ glued along their boundary spheres by a diffeomorphism $\varphi$.

steps.slogan: Extend the gluing map conewise to get a homeomorphism with $S^n$.
steps.detail: The map $\Phi(tx)=t\varphi(x)$ for $x\in S^{n-1}$ and $t\in[0,1]$ is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) of the ball extending $\varphi$. So $M$ is homeomorphic to two balls glued by the identity of their boundaries, which is $S^n$ (Alexander's trick).

concepts.c:closed-manifold: Compactness of $M$ gives the extremum points and a proper $f$.
concepts.c:morse-function: Nondegenerate critical points have normal forms by the Morse lemma.
concepts.c:critical-point: The two critical points are the extrema; no critical point lies between.
concepts.c:sphere: Two balls glued along their boundary form the sphere.
concepts.c:nondegenerate-critical-point: Nondegeneracy fixes the index and the local form of $f$.
concepts.c:diffeomorph: A diffeomorphism identifies the middle region with a product cylinder.
concepts.c:homeomorphism: The conewise extension is a homeomorphism of the ball, not a diffeomorphism.

source.note: Milnor, Morse Theory (1963), Theorem 4.1; the steps follow that proof.

statement: Let $P$ and $Q$ be [projections](c:projection) in a [von Neumann algebra](c:von-neumann-algebra) $M$. If each is Murray-von Neumann equivalent to a subprojection of the other, then $P\sim Q$: some partial isometry $T\in M$ has $T^*T=P$ and $TT^*=Q$.

hypotheses.text: $M$ is a [von Neumann algebra](c:von-neumann-algebra) and $P,Q\in M$ are [projections](c:projection).
A [partial isometry](c:partial-isometry) $V\in M$ has $V^*V=P$ and $VV^*\le Q$.
A partial isometry $W\in M$ has $W^*W=Q$ and $WW^*\le P$.

conclusion: A partial isometry $T\in M$ has $T^*T=P$ and $TT^*=Q$.

proofs.name: Orbit decomposition
proofs.slogan: Compose the two partial isometries, split off the orbit of the gap by a strongly convergent sum, and shift it, as in the set-theoretic proof.
proofs.scope: Projections of an arbitrary von Neumann algebra. Other analogs in the family, for other classes of operator algebras, are not covered.

roles.why: Strong closure of $M$ keeps the infinite sum of projections inside $M$.
The map $V$ sends $P$ into $Q$, which starts the composition.
The map $W$ sends $Q$ into $P$ and returns the result to $Q$.

steps.slogan: Compose $W$ and $V$ into one partial isometry $U$ of $P$ into itself.
steps.detail: Let $Q_1=VV^*\le Q$, so $QV=V$. Then $U=WV$ has $U^*U=V^*QV=P$ and $UU^*=WQ_1W^*\le WQW^*=F:=WW^*\le P$. Hence $P\sim UU^*\le F\le P$.

steps.slogan: Build the pairwise orthogonal projections $E_n=U^n(P-F)U^{*n}$.
steps.detail: With $R_n=U^nPU^{*n}$ decreasing, $E_n\le R_n-R_{n+1}$, so the $E_n$ are orthogonal. This replays the chain of the Cantor-Bernstein-Schroeder theorem. The strong sum $E=\sum_{n\ge0}E_n$ lies in $M$, satisfies $E\le P$, and $UE_n=E_{n+1}U$.

steps.slogan: Shift the orbit by $U$ and fix the rest to define $X$.
steps.detail: Put $X=(P-E)+UE$. Cross terms vanish because $UE$ has range under $E-E_0$, so $X^*X=(P-E)+E=P$ and $XX^*=(P-E)+(E-E_0)=P-E_0=F$. Hence $P\sim F$.

steps.slogan: Compose $X$ with $W^*$ to reach $Q$.
steps.detail: Let $T=W^*X$. Then $T^*T=X^*FX=P$ because $FX=X$, and $TT^*=W^*FW=W^*WW^*W=Q$. So $T\in M$ is a partial isometry with $T^*T=P$ and $TT^*=Q$, that is, $P\sim Q$.

concepts.c:projection: The statement and every step compare projections of $M$.
concepts.c:von-neumann-algebra: Strong closure keeps the infinite sum $E$ inside the algebra.
concepts.c:partial-isometry: Partial isometries carry the equivalences and compose.

source.note: Textbook proof (see Kadison and Ringrose, Fundamentals of the Theory of Operator Algebras, vol. II, ch. 6); it copies the Cantor-Bernstein chain argument.

statement: For a ring $R$, the stable $\infty$-category of unbounded [chain complexes](c:chain-complex) of $R$-modules, the [derived category](c:derived-category) $D(R)$, is equivalent to the $\infty$-category of [module spectra](c:module-spectrum) over the [Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum](c:eilenberg-maclane-spectrum) $HR$. For $R=\mathbb{Z}$ these are the $H\mathbb{Z}$-modules.

hypotheses.text: $R$ is an associative ring with unit.

conclusion: There is an equivalence $D(R)\simeq\mathrm{Mod}_{HR}$ of stable $\infty$-categories, induced by Quillen equivalences between chain complexes of $R$-modules and $HR$-module spectra.

proofs.name: Morita theory for stable model categories
proofs.slogan: Chain complexes form a stable model category with one compact generator whose endomorphism ring spectrum is $HR$, so Morita theory gives the equivalence.
proofs.scope: Every ring $R$; the abelian-group case $R=\mathbb{Z}$ is the nLab statement. The steps outline the cited paper.

roles.why: The ring $R$ is the compact generator and gives the endomorphism ring spectrum $HR$.

steps.slogan: Show that unbounded complexes form a stable model category with generator $R$.
steps.detail: [Chain complexes](c:chain-complex) of $R$-modules with quasi-isomorphisms form a stable, cofibrantly generated, proper model category. Suspension is the shift, and $R$ in degree $0$ is a compact generator.

steps.slogan: Apply Morita theory for stable model categories to the generator.
steps.detail: Schwede and Shipley show that a stable model category with one compact generator is Quillen equivalent to modules over the endomorphism ring spectrum of that generator.

steps.slogan: State the Dold-Kan correspondence at the simplicial level.
steps.detail: Dold-Kan identifies nonnegatively graded complexes of $R$-modules with simplicial $R$-modules. The stable statement is its stabilization, and the Eilenberg-MacLane functor is built on it.

steps.slogan: Identify the endomorphism ring spectrum of $R$ with $HR$.
steps.detail: The homotopy groups of the endomorphism spectrum are $\mathrm{Ext}^{-*}_R(R,R)$, which is $R$ in degree $0$ and zero elsewhere. A ring spectrum with this homotopy is $HR$, and Schwede and Shipley make the comparison with the [Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum](c:eilenberg-maclane-spectrum) explicit through Dold-Kan.

steps.slogan: Combine the Quillen equivalences and pass to underlying $\infty$-categories.
steps.detail: Chain complexes of $R$-modules and [module spectra](c:module-spectrum) over $HR$ are joined by a chain of Quillen equivalences. Their underlying $\infty$-categories agree, so $D(R)\simeq\mathrm{Mod}_{HR}$.

concepts.c:chain-complex: Unbounded complexes are one side of the equivalence.
concepts.c:derived-category: The derived category is the homotopy category of the complexes.
concepts.c:module-spectrum: Module spectra over $HR$ are the other side of the equivalence.
concepts.c:eilenberg-maclane-spectrum: It is the endomorphism ring spectrum of the generator $R$.

source.ref: S. Schwede and B. Shipley, Stable model categories are categories of modules, Topology 42 (2003), 103-153
source.note: Their Morita theorem and their comparison of chain complexes with modules over the Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum give the equivalence.

statement: The functor sending a [Stein space](c:stein-manifold) $X$ to the [Fréchet algebra](c:frechet-algebra) $\mathcal{O}(X)$ of holomorphic functions is fully faithful and contravariant: holomorphic maps $X\to Y$ correspond to algebra homomorphisms $\mathcal{O}(Y)\to\mathcal{O}(X)$. Its essential image is the category of Stein algebras, so Stein spaces are dual to Stein algebras.

hypotheses.text: $X$ and $Y$ are [Stein spaces](c:stein-manifold).

conclusion: The map $F\mapsto F^*$ from holomorphic maps $X\to Y$ to $\mathbb{C}$-algebra homomorphisms $\mathcal{O}(Y)\to\mathcal{O}(X)$ is a bijection, and the Stein algebras are exactly the algebras $\mathcal{O}(X)$.

proofs.name: Characters are points
proofs.slogan: Every character of the algebra of holomorphic functions on a Stein space is a point evaluation, so algebra maps become holomorphic maps of points.
proofs.scope: The contravariant functor on Stein spaces. The intrinsic axioms of Stein algebras, and later refinements such as holomorphically finitely generated algebras, are in the cited work and are not repeated.

roles.why: Holomorphic convexity and Cartan's theorems make characters into points and give local coordinates.

steps.slogan: Show that every character of $\mathcal{O}(Y)$ is a point evaluation.
steps.detail: Holomorphic convexity of the [Stein space](c:stein-manifold) $Y$ and Cartan's Theorem B (a Nullstellensatz for Stein spaces) show that a character $\chi$ whose kernel has no common zero would have $1$ in its kernel. So $\chi=\mathrm{ev}_y$ for one point $y$, and $y$ is unique because $\mathcal{O}(Y)$ separates points.

steps.slogan: Turn an algebra homomorphism into a map of points.
steps.detail: Let $\varphi\colon\mathcal{O}(Y)\to\mathcal{O}(X)$ be a homomorphism. For $x\in X$ the composite $\mathrm{ev}_x\circ\varphi$ is a character, so it equals $\mathrm{ev}_{F(x)}$ for a unique $F(x)\in Y$. Hence $\varphi(g)=g\circ F$ for every $g$.

steps.slogan: Prove that the map $F$ of points is holomorphic.
steps.detail: Functions in $\mathcal{O}(Y)$ give the topology and local coordinates of $Y$ (Cartan's Theorem A), and each $g\circ F=\varphi(g)$ is a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function). So $F$ is continuous and holomorphic.

steps.slogan: Show that pullback is a bijection on morphisms.
steps.detail: Pullback $F\mapsto F^*$ is injective because $\mathcal{O}(Y)$ separates points, and surjective by the previous two steps. It reverses composition, so $\mathcal{O}$ is a fully faithful contravariant functor.

steps.slogan: Name the essential image as the Stein algebras.
steps.detail: Forster characterizes the essential image intrinsically as the class of Stein [Fréchet algebras](c:frechet-algebra). So Stein spaces and Stein algebras form dual categories.

concepts.c:stein-manifold: Stein spaces are the geometric side of the duality.
concepts.c:frechet-algebra: The holomorphic functions form the Fréchet algebra on the algebraic side.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Pulled-back holomorphic functions make the map of points holomorphic.

source.ref: O. Forster, Zur Theorie der Steinschen Algebren und Moduln, Mathematische Zeitschrift 97 (1967), 376-405
source.note: Forster proves that the functor X to O(X) is a duality between Stein spaces and Stein algebras; the outline lists the main moves.

statement: Let $M$ be the centered Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator over Euclidean balls for [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) on $\mathbb{R}^n$. For each $p>1$ there is a constant $C_p$, independent of $n$, with $\|Mf\|_p\le C_p\|f\|_p$ for all $n$ and all $f$ in $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

hypotheses.text: $Mf(x)=\sup_{r>0}|B_r(x)|^{-1}\int_{B_r(x)}|f|$ uses Euclidean balls $B_r(x)$ and [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The exponent satisfies $p>1$.

conclusion: For every $n\ge1$ and every $f$, $\|Mf\|_{L^p}\le C_p\|f\|_{L^p}$ with $C_p$ depending only on $p$.

proofs.name: Spherical means and square functions
proofs.slogan: Dominate the ball averages by spherical means, bound them with square-function and multiplier methods on $L^2$, and extend the exponents, all with constants independent of $n$.
proofs.scope: The strong bound for $p>1$ on Euclidean balls. The same paper gives a weak type $(1,1)$ bound with constant $Cn\log n$ by a covering lemma, which is not outlined here; the steps rest on the cited paper.

roles.why: Radial averaging writes every ball average through spherical means, which the Fourier method treats.
The exponent range $p>1$ is reached by interpolation and the argument of the cited paper.

steps.slogan: Average spherical means to dominate the ball averages.
steps.detail: A ball average is a radial average of spherical means, $|B_t|^{-1}\int_{B_t}f=\int_0^1(\sigma_{rt}*f)\,nr^{n-1}\,dr$. So $Mf$ is at most the maximal function of the spherical means $\sigma_t*|f|$, which Stein treats by square-function methods.

steps.slogan: Bound the maximal means on $L^2$ with constants independent of $n$.
steps.detail: Following Stein, the cited paper splits the Fourier multiplier of the spherical mean by a Littlewood-Paley decomposition in the scale and estimates the resulting square functions with Bessel function bounds. All constants stay independent of $n$.

steps.slogan: Extend the bound to every exponent $p>1$.
steps.detail: Marcinkiewicz interpolation with the trivial $L^\infty$ bound gives all $p>2$. The range $1<p\le2$ needs the further argument of the cited paper, which also keeps the constants independent of $n$.

steps.slogan: Collect the bounds into one constant $C_p$.
steps.detail: For fixed $p>1$ the constants of the previous steps do not depend on $n$. So $\|Mf\|_p\le C_p\|f\|_p$ for all $n$ and all $f\in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, a bound on the [$L^p$ space](c:lp-space).

concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: Ball averages are taken against Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
concepts.c:lp-space: The theorem is a norm bound on $L^p$ with constant free of $n$.

source.ref: E. M. Stein and J.-O. Strömberg, Behavior of maximal functions in R^n for large n, Arkiv för Matematik 21 (1983), 259-269
source.note: Stein and Strömberg give the full proof; the outline lists its ingredients: spherical means, square functions and multipliers, and interpolation.

statement: Let $X$ be a [T1 space](c:t1-space), $D\subseteq X$ a [dense subspace](c:dense-subspace), $Y$ a [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space) and $f\colon D\to Y$ continuous. If $\overline{f^{-1}(A)}\cap\overline{f^{-1}(B)}=\emptyset$ in $X$ for all disjoint closed $A,B\subseteq Y$, then $f$ has a [continuous extension](c:continuous-extension) to $X$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a [T1 space](c:t1-space).
$D$ is a [dense subspace](c:dense-subspace) of $X$.
$Y$ is a [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space).
$f\colon D\to Y$ is continuous.
For all disjoint closed $A,B\subseteq Y$, the closures of $f^{-1}(A)$ and $f^{-1}(B)$ in $X$ are disjoint.

conclusion: There is a continuous map $F\colon X\to Y$ with $F|_D=f$.

proofs.name: Cluster sets
proofs.slogan: Define $F(x)$ as the unique cluster value of $f$ at $x$, and prove by compactness of $Y$ that $F$ is continuous.
proofs.scope: The stated direction. The converse is immediate: a continuous extension $F$ gives $\overline{f^{-1}(A)}\subseteq F^{-1}(A)$ for closed $A$.

roles.why: The cluster-set argument never uses the separation axiom of $X$.
Density makes every neighborhood of $x$ meet $D$ and fixes $F$ on $D$.
Compactness gives cluster points and continuity, and regularity gives separating closed sets.
The separation hypothesis already forces continuity of $f$, so the proof does not use it.
It rules out two different cluster values at one point.

steps.slogan: Collect the cluster values of $f$ at each point of $X$.
steps.detail: For $x\in X$ let $L(x)=\bigcap_U\overline{f(U\cap D)}$ over the open [neighborhoods](c:neighborhood) $U$ of $x$. Density gives $U\cap D\ne\emptyset$, so these closed subsets of the compact space $Y$ have the finite intersection property and $L(x)\ne\emptyset$.

steps.slogan: Show that each cluster set has exactly one point.
steps.detail: Suppose $y_1\ne y_2$ lie in $L(x)$. As $Y$ is [regular](c:regular-space), pick disjoint closed $A,B$ with $y_1\in\mathrm{int}A$ and $y_2\in\mathrm{int}B$. Every neighborhood of $x$ meets $f^{-1}(A)$ and $f^{-1}(B)$, so $x$ lies in both [closures](c:closure), against the separation hypothesis.

steps.slogan: Define $F(x)$ as the point of $L(x)$ and check that $F$ extends $f$.
steps.detail: For $x\in D$ the point $f(x)$ lies in $\overline{f(U\cap D)}$ for every $U$, so $f(x)\in L(x)=\{F(x)\}$. Hence $F(x)=f(x)$.

steps.slogan: Prove that $F$ is continuous by compactness of $Y$.
steps.detail: Let $V$ be open with $F(x)\in V$, and pick open $W$ with $F(x)\in W\subseteq\overline W\subseteq V$. The closed sets $\overline{f(U\cap D)}$ form a downward directed family with intersection $\{F(x)\}\subseteq W$, so one of them lies in $W$. For $x'$ in the interior of that $U$, we get $F(x')\in\overline{f(U\cap D)}\subseteq V$.

concepts.c:t1-space: The hypothesis is stated but this argument does not need it.
concepts.c:dense-subspace: Density makes the cluster sets nonempty and pins down $F$ on $D$.
concepts.c:compact-hausdorff-space: Compactness and regularity of $Y$ give cluster points and continuity.
concepts.c:continuous-extension: The map $F$ is the required continuous extension of $f$.
concepts.c:neighborhood: Cluster values are defined through neighborhoods of the point.
concepts.c:regular-space: Regularity separates two points of $Y$ by disjoint closed sets.
concepts.c:closure: The separation hypothesis speaks about closures of preimages.

source.note: Direct cluster-set argument; the theorem is due to A. D. Taimanov.

statement: If finitely many planks, closed regions between two parallel [hyperplanes](c:hyperplane), cover a [convex body](c:convex-body) $K\subset\mathbb{R}^d$, then the sum of the plank widths is at least the minimal width $w(K)$ of $K$.

hypotheses.text: $K\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ is a [convex body](c:convex-body) with minimal width $w(K)=\min_{|u|=1}(h_K(u)+h_K(-u))$, where $h_K$ is its support function.
The planks $P_1,\dots,P_m$ cover $K$, and $P_j$ has width $w_j$, the distance between its two bounding hyperplanes.

proofs.name: Width vectors and signs
proofs.slogan: Give each plank a width vector, choose signs so that the signed sum avoids every open plank, and fit that sum inside the body.
proofs.scope: Finite families of planks in any dimension $d\ge1$. Bang's conjecture on relative widths is open and is not covered.

roles.why: The minimal width of the body is what lets the signed sum fit inside it.
The covering planks, widened, give the vectors $a_je_j$ and the final contradiction.

steps.slogan: Assume the widths sum to less than $w(K)$ and widen the planks.
steps.detail: Suppose $\sum w_j<w(K)$ and choose $\delta>0$ with $\sum(w_j+\delta)<w(K)$. Replace $P_j$ by the open plank $\{x:|\langle x,e_j\rangle-c_j|<a_j\}$ with $|e_j|=1$ and $a_j=(w_j+\delta)/2$. These planks still cover $K$, and $s=\sum a_j<w(K)/2$.

steps.slogan: Choose signs by maximizing a quadratic function over the cube.
steps.detail: Fix $x_0$ and put $y_\varepsilon=x_0+\sum\varepsilon_ja_je_j$. Let $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}^m$ maximize $\Phi=\tfrac12|\sum\varepsilon_ja_je_j|^2+\sum\varepsilon_ja_j(\langle x_0,e_j\rangle-c_j)$. Flipping $\varepsilon_j$ changes $\Phi$ by $-2\varepsilon_ja_jg_j+2a_j^2\le0$, where $g_j=\langle y_\varepsilon,e_j\rangle-c_j$. So $|g_j|\ge a_j$ and $y_\varepsilon$ lies in no open plank.

steps.slogan: Reduce the fitting of a zonotope in $K$ to a system of inequalities.
steps.detail: Let $Z=\{\sum t_ja_je_j:|t_j|\le1\}$, so $h_Z(u)=\sum a_j|\langle e_j,u\rangle|$. Then $x_0+Z\subseteq K$ iff $\langle x_0,u\rangle\le h_K(u)-h_Z(u)$ for all unit $u$. By Farkas' lemma a finite subsystem is solvable if $\sum\lambda_i(h_K(u_i)-h_Z(u_i))\ge0$ whenever $\lambda_i\ge0$ and $\sum\lambda_iu_i=0$. Bounds on the coordinates and compactness then give one $x_0$.

steps.slogan: Check the Farkas condition with the minimal width.
steps.detail: Fix $j$ and let $p_j=\sum\lambda_iu_i$ over the $i$ with $\langle e_j,u_i\rangle>0$. Then $\sum_i\lambda_i|\langle e_j,u_i\rangle|=2\langle e_j,p_j\rangle\le2|p_j|$, and $L=\sum\lambda_ih_K(u_i)\ge h_K(p_j)+h_K(-p_j)\ge w(K)|p_j|$. So $\sum\lambda_ih_Z(u_i)\le\sum_j2a_j|p_j|\le(2s/w(K))L\le L$, because $L\ge h_K(0)=0$.

steps.slogan: Place the sign sum inside $K$ and contradict the covering.
steps.detail: Take $x_0$ with $x_0+Z\subseteq K$, and take $\varepsilon$ from the sign step for this $x_0$. The point $y_\varepsilon$ lies in $x_0+Z\subseteq K$ and in no open plank, against the covering. So $\sum w_j\ge w(K)$.

concepts.c:convex-body: The body has a minimal width, which the planks must reach.
concepts.c:hyperplane: Each plank is bounded by two parallel hyperplanes with unit normal $e_j$.

source.note: Strategy of T. Bang, A solution of the plank problem, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 2 (1951), 990-993: width vectors, signs and a signed sum outside all open planks. The sign lemma and the fitting lemma are proved here.

statement: Let $ABC$ be a [triangle](c:triangle) and $P_0$ a point of the side $AB$. Draw from $P_0$ a segment [parallel](c:parallel-lines) to $BC$ to $P_1$ on $AC$, then parallel to $AB$ to $P_2$ on $BC$, then parallel to $CA$ to $P_3$ on $AB$. Repeat the three directions to reach $P_4$ on $AC$, $P_5$ on $BC$ and $P_6$ on $AB$. Then $P_6=P_0$.

hypotheses.text: $ABC$ is a nondegenerate [triangle](c:triangle).
The start point $P_0$ lies on the side $AB$.

proofs.name: Affine coordinates
proofs.slogan: An affine map reduces the claim to the standard triangle, where the six points are computed and $P_6=P_0$ appears.
proofs.scope: All triangles and all start points. At a vertex some segments have length zero, and the path still closes.

roles.why: Every triangle is the affine image of the standard triangle.
The start point has one parameter $a$ that determines all six points.

steps.slogan: Reduce to the standard triangle by an affine map.
steps.detail: An affine map carries any triangle onto $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $C=(0,1)$, and it keeps [parallel lines](c:parallel-lines), sides and incidences. So it is enough to prove the claim for this triangle.

steps.slogan: Compute the points $P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$ in coordinates.
steps.detail: Let $P_0=(a,0)$ with $0\le a\le1$. The line through $P_0$ parallel to $BC$ is $x+y=a$, which meets $AC$ at $P_1=(0,a)$. The line $y=a$ meets $BC$ at $P_2=(1-a,a)$, and the line $x=1-a$ meets $AB$ at $P_3=(1-a,0)$.

steps.slogan: Repeat the computation from $P_3$ to find $P_4$, $P_5$ and $P_6$.
steps.detail: The point $P_3$ is on $AB$ with parameter $1-a$, so the same rules give $P_4=(0,1-a)$, $P_5=(a,1-a)$ and $P_6=(a,0)$.

steps.slogan: Compare $P_6$ with $P_0$ and transfer the result back.
steps.detail: We found $P_6=(a,0)=P_0$. The affine map preserves the whole construction, so the path closes in every triangle.

concepts.c:triangle: Every triangle is affinely equivalent to the standard one.
concepts.c:parallel-lines: Affine maps keep parallel lines, so the construction transfers.

source.note: Affine coordinates on the standard triangle.
